subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE OF THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Just a moment or two prior to the opening of the House, we, the members of the House and others, were favoured with a very brief, all too brief, exhibition of singing, a rendering of the sweetest of music by the visiting choir from the old land, and I thought that, as the first member of the House to speak following that interesting occasion, it would not be out of place to express my personal appreciation of the splendid manner in which they rendered the various numbers on their program an expression which I am sure will be shared by others, and to extend to Mr. Sydney H. Nicholson, the organist, and the Rev. Edmund
H.	Fellowes, the director of the choir, our sincere and cordial felicitations.
It might properly be hinted to me that the atmosphere created by that pleasing incident is not quite fitting to a debate upon the hard and material facts which are supposed to be dealt with in a budget. Indeed one of my very good friends from the other side of the House, knowing that I was about to speak, intimated to me very kindly that there should be no bitterness left in my soul. I wish to assure the House that there is no bitterness in my soul now or on any other occasion when I am dealing with subjects such as we have before us this afternoon pertaining to the business of the country. After all, it is the business of members of the opposition to take up government measures or proposals and subject them to the most critical analysis that we are capable of, and if there are weaknesses in them to expose those weaknesses. On the other hand it is our privilege, if not our duty, to differ from those who differ from us, and, in so far as the views we hold are honest and honourable, to advance those views with all the vigour and force of which we are capable, and to-day I intend to follow the course which I have followed in the seventeen sessions I have been in this House by dealing with this subject, I hope fairly, but with that degree of energy with which a kind Providence may have blest me.
We have immediately before us a resolution that this House shall resolve itself into a committee of ways and means, with an amendment thereto moved1 by my hon. friend from Macleod (Mr. Coote), making one or two suggestions. With this amendment I find myself able very largely to agree. I certainly do not agree with all of it. I would not hare worded it in exactly this manner, but
The Budget-Mr. Stevens

with much of the sentiment in the resolution I find myself in accord. I will just briefly deal with the amendment, but as the major part of my remarks will be directed to other subjects, I shall not spend more than a moment or two on the amendment. I may say that the last clause of the amendment is the only explicit and clear statement. The balance of the amendment is more or less of an expedient, a grouping of words, calculated, I think, to embarrass some, and to give expression to certain views not too clearly, indeed somewhat ambiguously. But the last clause reads as follows:
And further that no systematic effort is being made to reduce our national debt, the interest on which absorbs so large a proportion of the revenues of the Dominion.
I	intend to deal with that question in a moment, and I find myself entirely in accord with this: that the government should be brought to task for not having dealt with the question of the public debt in a little more definite and efficient manner than they have done. In regard to the balance of the resolution, it refers to the reduction in the high cost of living. This is a term that is used very, very frequently in this House, on the hustings and elsewhere. It is a popular cry, it has a strong appeal on the hustings, politicians like to use it, and I have no particular criticism of it. But I would point out to the House that the high cost of living, according to our view, is not merely the price of goods. It involves also whether or not a man can make a living at all, whether or not he has an opportunity to work. It is of infinitely greater importance to our people that they shall have an opportunity to earn rather than to be given the cost of living figures of to-day as compared with those of a month or a year ago. So I find no great difficulty in facing that clause, because the policy I stand .behind to-day and have been standing behind for years is a policy calculated to give Canadians a maximum of employment within the bounds of their own country and the highest standard of living. So I repeat, I have no difficulty in satisfying myself that we are able to offer to the people a policy which will give them the maximum of comfort in so far as it refers to the cost of living.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I wish to turn my attention to the main subject, namely, the committee of ways and means. I think it was Sir Robert Peel who, on one occasion when facing an exceedingly difficult and perplexing crisis in the financial affairs of the old land, said that half of the task was accomplished when you frankly faced the question. That is, if this House will consider and study the problems

with which the country is faced and frankly look them in the eye, half the solution is arrived at. And so this afternoon I shall address myself very largely to bringing to the atten-ion of the House three major problems. These major problems I intend to analyze in some degree, and for this purpose I am going to take five-year periods. The Minister of Railways (Mr. Dunning) is not in his seat. Last night he invited us to consider the five years of Liberal rule, and in doing so he suggested that there had been a progression of events leading to some definite conclusion. I propose to examine this five-year period, and tq place it in juxtaposition with the five-year period preceding, so that we may get a clear vision whether or not this country is progressing, as some claim, and to what degree that progress is of value or may be measured.
Among the institutions that we have inherited from the old land is the parliamentary system of government. A subdivision of that is the budget system, generally, I think, admitted by all to be the most effective method of dealing with the financial, trade and other affairs of the nation. This budget system is supposed to give to parliament certain information. For instance, it is supposed to deal with our financial condition, that is, our debts to our own people and to other nations; it is supposed also to deal with the question of taxation, that is, the revenues secured during the past year and the proposed methods of raising those revenues in the future, together with whatever taxation changes may be contemplated; in addition to that, it usually outlines for the information of the people the conditions of industry and trade, both internal and external. It is my intention to deal with these three phases of our country's affairs.
In the first place, I wish to say to the Minister of Finance that much as I appreciate his geniality and all those fine qualities that we so much admire in him, in my opinion his budget fails adequately to reflect the real conditions of the country. This budget does not budget for the future; it offers no new ideas; it is a static budget, it is dormant, it is stationary; it shows no progress, it offers no hope, it does not look into the future or give to us any idea that the government has the slightest appreciation of the rapidly changing world conditions, or that there are certain conditions in this country calling for new or different treatment from that of the past; it offers nothing in the way of suggestion as to the replacement of our depleted natural resources; it does not indicate that the government is giving that problem the slightest consideration, the necessity of which I hope to demonstrate in the course of my

The Budget-Mr. Stevens
remarks. I say to the minister also that it is a misleading budget. It is full of equivocations. It announces, for instance, a reduced duty-there is no reduction in duty; it announces lower taxation-there is an increase of taxatisn; it announces a surplus-this surplus is a myth; it also states that there is abounding business-this is only partially true. '
The budget, however, is consistent in one respect-it reflects a complete abandonment of the pre-election pledges of the Liberal party. I have only to call the attention of the Minister of Finance and his colleagues to the remarks of the hon. member for La-belle (Mr. Bourassa) yesterday afternoon, when he unfolded the inside secrets of the Liberal party and reminded us that ?omc years ago when that party went to the country with certain views that it persuaded the people to adopt, it carried on the old fiscal policy, slightly modified here and there, but in principle the policy of Sir John Macdonald, and that secret assurances prior to the election were given to the business interests of the country that the public utterances of the party would not be given effect to afterwards should it be successful at the polls. And so I say now we come to a very similar condition: the pre-election pledges of the Liberal party are not reflected in the budget. Not that we ask that they should be; but we do ask, Mr. Speaker, with some degree of right, that a party which led the people to believe that a given set of results would follow from a given set of actions should at least carry out its pledges on the faith of which it has received a mandate from the electorate, whether those principles are right, or whether other principles adopted in the place of those abandoned are not really the right principles.
Last night the Minister of Railways was very fulsome in his praise of the Minister of Finance for having brought down his budget so early. To my mind this suggests just a little clever political strategy. The Minister of Finance smiles, but he knows it is true. He had the Duncan report on the maritime provinces before him. The government had it in their sanctum over in the east block. They studied it and they divided on it, and they are divided on it to-day, as everybody knows. They are in a dilemma regarding that report. It calls for certain things which ought to be in this budget but the government dare not put them in this budget.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Another minister	says
"hear, hear." You will observe they are ministers who say that. Well, the budget has been welcomed throughout the country, because it was feared that following on the preelection declarations of the government, particularly in western Canada, there would be drastic changes in the tariff when the budget was brought down. But that apprehension has been allayed, for there are no great changes in the tariff, and so a sigh of relief has gone up from one end of the country to the other. A safe hand, it is felt, is at the throttle. There is no danger to industry. Everything is promising because the tariff has not been tampered with. Let me read the words of the Bank of Montreal issued in their official private bulletin of February 23:
The early delivery of the budget speech by the Dominion Minister of Finance, and the announcement that no tariff changes are to be made, should be helpful to business by removing that uncertainty and hesitancy in mercantile transactions which sometimes wait upon the late pronouncement of government fiscal policy.
Yes, the budget was welcomed for what it did not do, not for anything that it did. We welcome it in so far as in it the government has stayed its hand in further reductions of the tariff. The government announces in the budget that it is not its intention this year utterly to destroy the remaining fragment of a protective principle in the tariff. In other words, they have given the protective policy a tentative reprieve from the hangman's noose.
This is called a Robb budget, and I use that term without any personal reference to the minister. It is indeed a rob budget in the sense that it robs Peter to pay Paul. It is a budget which announces a reduction of taxation while as a matter of fact there is just
The Budget-Mr. Stevens

a slight shifting of the burden of taxation. The taxation may be lowered in some small respects here and there, but the net result is an increase, as I shall well demonstrate in a moment. Let me deal with the budget, or rather the budget subject, because the budget itself would not require very much treatment. I pointed out a moment ago that the ways and means committee would have under its consideration normally the question of debt, the question of revenue, or the levying of taxation, and the question of trade conditions; and I intend to examine the whole subjeot in that order.
In the first place, I will discuss the debt. The minister announced that there would be a reduction in the debt, and in this connection I desire to bring to the attention of the House a singular fact. I have here the figures from each of four speeches delivered by the present Minister of Finance, and I will read them all to the House. On April 10, 1924, he said our surplus would be $20,750,000, to be applied to the reduction of the public debt. On March 24, 1925, he said that the public debt had been decreased by $35,900,000. On April 15, 1926, the minister informed the House, there had been a reduction in the debt of $22,350,000. On February 17, 1927, at page 387 of Hansard . the minister made the statement that there would be a reduction of $31,000,000 in our debt.
The individual reductions indicated iin these four announcements total $110,000,000, so that there should be a reduction in the debt to that extent from the year 1922. Each year this government has officially announced a reduction to the amount I have quoted, the total being $110,000,000; and bearing that in mind I would ask hon. members to follow me in an analysis of the public debt. There are two terms used in referring to the debt: one, the net debt, is the popular expression; the other is the funded debt, or, as my hon. friend from West Calgary (Mr. Bennett) described it, the dead weight debt. I myself prefer to call it the mortgage debt of the country. Now, the term "net debt" is a misnomer; it is meaningless. I hold in my hands the Public Accounts of the years between 1922 and 1926.
I take for purposes of illustration the latter year. In the Public Accounts, on page 3, will be found the balance sheet of the Dominion of Canada, and I would invite every hon. gentleman who has any knowledge of accountancy to examine that statement. What do we find in it? We find among the assets certain sums mentioned under various headings. For example, there

is "cash on hand." What does that represent? It means simply current cash that happens to be in the hands of scores of the representatives of the government throughout the Dominion, and so far as it has any relation to the reduction of the debt, it does not amount to the snap of the finger. It may be needed to-morrow; it is simply cash in the till carried from day to day, and represents no resources from which the funded debt may be paid. We might term it "petty cash " Then there is "specie reserve;" that is the gold reserve kept in the treasury in Ottawa against Dominion notes. That is something that cannot very well be used for the reduction of the fixed debt. Again, there are advances to the banks under the Finance Act; that merely refers to the fluctuating loans to the banks under that act to help the business of the country.
On the other side you have a certain amount of liabilities, including various items such as trust funds, post office money orders, outstanding Dominion notes in circulation, and so forth. The point I make is this: after subtracting the liabilities from the assets there is a net balance shown which is referred to as the net debt of the country, but which I submit has no relation whatsoever to the real debt. It is merely a balance between your assets and your liabilities, merely a bookkeeping sum; it is nothing more nor less than, a means of keeping a double entry set of books in order. Now I take the funded debt, schedule (t), which gives the sum of $2,471,000,000. However, before I discuss the funded debt I will make a further reference or two to what is called the net debt. I find that the net debt on March 31, 1922, was $2,422,000,000 and on December 31, 1926, including the amount paid off last fall, it was $2,343,000,000; that is to say, we have a reduction in the net debt of $79,000,000, in a period of five years. That' is nothing for this country to be proud of. I ask, where is the $110,000,000 of a reduction in the debt as announced by the Minister of.Finance officially year by year? It is not reflected in these figures; it cannot be found in the blue books; it is not there. It is a myth. But stranger still, I find that as between the 1922 reports and the Public Accounts of 1926, there has been a reduction in the circulation of Dominion notes of $58,880,000, which forms a part of this $79,000,000 reduction in the net debt. Let me put a question to my friends from the west who for the last ten years have been quite serious in their economic studies. Do they consider that a re-

The Budget-Mr. Stevens
duction in the circulation of Dominion notes is of any great advantage to the Business of this country?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: No.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE OF THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Here are the figures, and this is part of the $79,000,000 of which they boast; I will come to the funded debt in a moment and show an even more deplorable condition there. In 1922 the Dominion notes in circulation amounted to $241,000,000 in round figures, while in 1926 they amounted to something over $182,000,000, or a reduction of $58,880,000. What does this mean? We have a Finance Act which in Canada corresponds to the federal reserve system of the United States, in a somewhat modified form, and hon. members will recall that in the revision of the Bank Act in 1923 this point was advanced as the reason why we should not establish a federal reserve bank in Canada.
I took that view then and I still hold to it, but I ask that the Finance Act should function; I ask that the advantages and powers of that Finance Act be put into operation, and the figures to which I have just referred indicate that under the Finance Aot the circulation of Dominion notes is less by $58,880,000 than it was in 1922, with a corresponding retardation of current business in the country.

speechtext: Might I ask a question, just for information? Does the hon. gentleman attribute that decrease to the disposition on the part of the banks to refrain from offering for discount their own particular securities?

They can very readily attract attention to this facility and encourage the banks and others to utilize this accommodation which is at their disposal.

speechtext: Before my friend leaves that point, I suppose he will admit now that Canadian currency is on a sounder basis than it was during the earlier period to which he was referring, when Canadian funds in New York were at a 16 per cent discount?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE OF THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
No one has more regard
for the minister than myself, but with all due respect to him that is not an intelligent interjection, and the minister knows that it is
not; he is simply drawing a red herring across the trail. The discount to which our money was subjected was due to extraordinary world causes entirely, and not to Canadian causes. Now I will give the minister a further answer:
I was just looking for further figures when he interrupted me. The situation is that we needed this money to bolster up our credit. In 1922 we had $241,000,000 of Dominion notes in circulation, with a specie reserve of $85,000,000; to-day we have a specie reserve of $99,000,000 with a Dominion note circulation of $182,000,000. In other words, we have now a specie reserve of about 54 per cent as against about 35 per cent in 1922; I had the figures here somewhere but they have been mislaid. There is no excuse for that; we could very easily increase our Dominion note circulation without the slightest chance of jeopardizing the stability of our currency.
Now I turn to the funded debt, which is the real debt of the country, our inescapable obligations. These are the obligations this country has signed, sealed and delivered to the public of Canada or to the public of the world, and I want the House to examine this question for a moment with me. I have the figures from 1922 to 1926, varying from $2,420,000,000, in 1922, to $2,471,000,000 in 1926, or an increase in our funded debt in that period of $51,000,000. If you deduct from that the amount of $35,000,000 paid off last year, you have a net increase to date in our funded debt of $16,000,000. Where is the $110,000,000 which was announced as a reduction of the public debt? I saw great headlines in newspaper all over the country; I had not time to dig them up and bring them here, but they would have made interesting pictures: "Robb reduces the public debt $20,000,000," or $35,000,000, $22,000,000, $31,000,000! Every year this has been heralded throughout the country as a great accomplishment of this government, but nere are the figures taken from the government's own books, the report of the Auditor General, showing a net increase in that five year period in our mortgage debt of $16,000,-
000.
That is not all; in addition to that amount of $2,471,000,000 there are the railway guarantees of $658,000,000. But someone will say, "Oh, we have great assets to offset that." Let us see if that is so. What are our obligations to the National railways, or let me put it in another way; what have we put into the railways of this country? According to the annual report of this government, Mr. Speaker, we have put into the railways no less than $1,113,590,000 in cash, plus the guarantees of $658,000,000 or a total of about
The Budget-Mr. Stevens

$1,770,000,000. Do not say to me that in connection with this railway obligation we have a magnificent asset. It is true that we have an asset, but we also have an investment of $1,770,000,000. Now I will return to my starting point; in addition to the ordinary funded debt we have these railway guarantees of $658,000,000, just as serious an obligation on this country as any other. And what if it came to a revaluation? Where is the Minister of Immigration (Mr. Forke) now, he who was so anxious to interrupt me a moment ago? He has fled the chamber. Where is the policy of the Minister of Immigration, which he announced year after year when he sat to my left; where is his policy of revaluation of the National railways, now that he is on the other side of the House? I say to him and to this House that if the National railways were revalued the result would in all probability show a difference between our investment and the revaluation of a sum approximating this item of guarantees, namely $658,000,000. So for all practical purposes this amount should be added to the funded debt of this country, which would give a total of $3,129,000,000 as our real debt, instead of $2,400,000,000 as given by the Minister of Finance.
Now I wish to turn my attention to the question of taxation, and before commencing I may say that I wish to address myself in some measure to the Minister of Immigration, who is not in his seat. I may say that I advised him a few moments ago before he ieft the House that I was going to do so, so that he has no excuse for saying later on that I attacked him in his absence.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: He is the minister of migration.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE OF THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I said a little while ago that one of the subjects that should have been discussed in this budget, as in all budgets, is the question of taxation. I hold in my hand certain announced surpluses claimed by this government. My hon. friends opposite in 1924 announced a surplus of $35,990,000; in 1925', they announced a surplus of $24,300,000; in 1926, they announced a surplus of $33,910,000; and in 1927, they announced a surplus of $34,200,000, or a total of $128,400,000. I ask again, as I have asked in the case of that mythical reduction of the public debt, where are these surpluses? Oh, someone will say, they are applied to the reduction of the national debt. No, they were not. These are accountancy terms, bookkeepers' terms, to balance current accounts, and for the life of me I cannot see the justification of it. But the minister told 
us the other day-and he did it in that quiet, gentle way, which is peculiar to him and which I think won the hearts of a great many people in the last election; I hope they will have awakened from their sleep, the result of his seductive terms-"I am pleased to announce a further reduction in taxation of $27,000,000." He said the same thing before; he said it last year. My bon. friends from the extreme left to the right on the other side of the House have used this as one of the strongest arguments to support this government-" reduction in taxation ".
Well now, what are taxes? Taxes are simply the various returns from certain sources of revenue which we have. My hon. friends from the west, who are of strong free trade tendencies, always refer to the customs duty as a tax. No one will deny that the sales tax is a tax; no one will for a moment say that the income tax is not a tax; no one will say that the various stamp impositions are not taxes. All of these are taxes. Indeed our revenue from top to bottom, and from one side to the other, is taxation. Now let us see what reductions we have had in taxation. I take the five years just past, from 1923 to 1927, and the average imposition of taxes of this kind by this government was $387,7SO.OOO. In the previous years under the Conservative government the average was $348,500,000, or an increase of $39,280,000 in the average of the last five years over the previous five years. In other words, it is a ten per cent increase of taxation taking the average of the last five years as against the average for the previous five years. Now what I want to say is this: We have been told year by year that taxes are being reduced.
I said at the opening of my remarks that the Minister of Finance had not reduced taxes, he had merely shifted them, and that is precisely what has occurred. What did he do last year? Oh, they say, he lowered the tax on automobiles. Let us see if he did. He reduced the tax on automobiles when he introduced liia budget. Then came three thousand workers from Oshawa to make representations to this parliament, and my hon. friend and his colleagues prayed earnestly day by day that the debate might be carried on, and they carried it on for five weeks. In the interim they revamped their budget, they changed the whole business. They shifted the burden of taxation round a bit first so as to drive certain industries out of business and save the industry which at first was threatened by the reduction of the tariff, and the automobile industry at the conclusion of the deal that was made, was better off than

The Budget-Mr. Stevens
it was before. With what results? There was an increase in revenue from goods coming in from the other side whereas hundreds of persons in Canada were thrown out of business. But the point I am making is that the taxes imposed during the last five years are ten per cent higher than the taxes codlected in the five years preceding their accession to office.
Now the Minister of Railways (Mr. Dunning) said last night "They say this is a Tory budget. Does anybody doubt which is the high tariff party and which the low tariff party?" I did not hear very much noise on the other side in response to that. I think there was a good deal of doubt in their minds as to the wisdom of the Minister of Railways making that statement. The minister said, "No one doubts which is the high tariff party and which is the low tariff party." I purpose discovering this afternoon something regarding this high tariff party. The Minister of Railways said also that since 1921 the tariff has been lowered in many important particulars. There was a certain lowering here and a certain lowering there which I shall deal with, but these changes certainly did not result in a lowering of the taxation on the people of Canada. There have been three major changes in the tariff since this government took office in 1921. There was a change in 1922-23 in the woollen schedule; there was a change in 1923-24 in the iron and steel schedule, chiefly regarding agricultural implements and subsidiary industries; and the change last year in regard to the automobile industry. I intend to examine briefly the exact effects these changes have had on the industry of Canada, and I wish the House to follow my analysis with some care because I believe it will offer rather startling results.
Before doing that, however, I wish to deal with this hi^h tariff-low tariff bogy. My hon. friend, the Minister of Agriculture, trots out the bogy of high tariff every once in a while. How he fulminated against this party a few years ago on account, as he said, of our high tariff tendencies, and how he declared, "Why, the Liberal party, the Mackenzie King government, were just making a beginning." But along came some skilful hand that turned aside his mad charge against protection, the skilful hand of the Minister of Finance, and left my hon. friend bellowing up a blind alley. Then we come to the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Stewart). He had hold of the rope attached to the bell to toll it. He said, "I am sounding the death knell of protection," and he yanked away on this rope. Suddenly he woke up with the frayed end of the rope in his hand, and the bell stopped tolling. He
found also that some mysterious hand had slipped in and cut the rope. It was the hand of the Minister of Finance that turned aside this other doughty warrior from carrying on his assaults. Here lies the body-
Political body, of course,

My hon. friend a moment ago thumped his desk vigorously when I referred to that part of his resolution which dealt with the protective principles ^of the tariff. Will he say, or will any other hon. member on that side, say that there is any less protection in the tariff than there was six years ago or five years ago?
I	am going to examine, for the benefit of this House, the figures and facts in regard to this matter, and in this regard I take them from the government's own productions, which I have on my desk. I am not going to read all the figures, but I have a table showing the dutiable and the free imports, with the totals, the amounts collected, and the per cent dutiable and the per cent free. I have it over a period of ten years and it shows the following result. I will give the two five-year periods first.
The average rate of duty during the last five years of Conservative rule, 1918 to 1922 inclusive, was on dutiable goods, 22.1 per cent, and on dutiable and free goods, 13.2 per cent. During the last five years under Liberal rule, 1923 to 1927, the percentage of duty on dutiable goods was 24 per cent and the percentage on dutiable and free goods, 15.5 per cent.

The Budget-Mr. Stevens
In other words, during the last five years the rate of duty on dutiable goods was 2 per cent higher than it was during the previous five years, and the rate on dutiable and free goods was 2.3 per cent higher. But someone will say to me: Oh, but during the last year or two we have been lowering the tariff. Let us see. Let the House bear in mind the observation I have already made on two occasions, that there has been going on, not a lowering, but a shifting of taxation. In 1921 the percentage on dutiable goods was 20.6 per cent; in 1926 the percentage of duty on dutiable goods was 24.7 per cent; or in other words, it is higher this year than it has been in any single year in the last ten years with the exception of 1923. In other words the rate of duty charged by the tariff of this country has not been reduced at all. We do not quarrel with that. What we do quarrel with is that this government and its followers, the Minister of Immigration, the Minister of the Interior, the Minister of Agriculture, and others, when it suits their purposes, go to the country and declare that they have lowered the tariff, the customs duties, whereas as a matter of fact the cold figures show that if there has been any change at all, there has been a slight increase. Then they say that the Tories maintain a protective tariff but they eschew protection. There is exactly the same protection in the tariff to-day as there was prior to 1921; in fact a little more.

In the year 1922 there were imported into Canada 12,000,000 pounds of wool. There was a domestic production of 20,000,000 pounds, and there was retained in Canada 32,000,000 pounds. That is the amount of domestic and imported wool retained in Canada. In 1926 there was imported and retained a volume of 13,000,000 pounds; there was raised and retained 9,000,000 pounds-a total of only 22,000,000 pounds. In other words, owing to the reduction in the duty on goods comprised in the woollen schedule there was a reduction in the use of wool in Canada, imported and domestic, of over 10,000,000 pounds. The use of Canadian wool in these manufactures dropped from 20,000,000 to 9,000.000 pounds.
I have held the view for many years that our agricultural industry would be infinitely better off if wool production was added to its general activities. It is admitted by all expert agriculturists, I think, that this is sound policy. And yet we have in vogue a tariff policy which i3 discouraging the production of domestic wool-a policy indeed which has resulted in a drop of the production of domestic wool for weaving in Canada of over 10,000,000 pounds, or more than 55 per cent.
Now I want to show another phase of this subject-wages. This affects the workers of Canada. My hon. friend asked: Why cannot Canada produce just as cheaply as Great Britain or any other country? And they add: If our manufacturers cannot do so then they are not entitled to any consideration. That, I admit, is a bald, crude statement, but it is really the argument that is advanced. I will give the House now the reason why our manufacturers cannot produce as cheaply as the manufacturers of Great Britain, and I challenge any hon. member seriously to attempt to controvert these facts as far as they relate to Canada. I have under my hand the whole list of labour engaged in the woollen spinning trade. Let me give the average percentages for the information of hon. members.
For this class of workers the average wage paid in England is $8.65 per week, in Canada it is $16.35. Fifty-five per cent of the cost of a woollen article is in wages. That being the case, it requires a duty of at least 27+ per cent before you put the Canadian spinner on an equal footing with the British spinner.
In other words, if you put aside the tariff altogether you would give to the British spinner a premium of 27i per cent. Someone wilj say: Well, cannot you lower the wages of the Canadian spinner? There are certain reasons why we cannot. First, we do not wish to lower the standard of living. I do not think anyone will challenge that. But there is another reason, which is obligatory in its character. The main provinces that are affected, Ontario principally, have what they call a minimum wage law. This law has been placed on the statute books of the provinces as the result of public opinion that the workers in these factories are entitled to a certain minimum wage. That minimum wage corresponds very closely to this $16.35-not exactly. But I say, if you reduce wages in Canada to a point equivalent to the wages of their competitors in Europe, then you would go below the scale provided by the minimum wage law.

ports are raw materials, chiefly ore. Take asbestos; we are selling $7,000,000 worth of asbestos to the United States to be turned into $70,000,000 worth of products. It emanates from three sources almost entirely; pulp and paper, in which there has been a tremendous increase; the development of electrical energy and in northern Ontario and Quebec the mining boom. I wanted to discuss briefly the three points upon which I claimed there has been activity. One has to do with water powers. I have intimated already that there was an effort made to secure the export of Canadian power to the United States and this is what I desired to say further:	The
development of electrical energy is one of the most vital needs of the country to-day, in view of the modern methods of manufacture, when Canada is peculiarly blest with great water powers, and the one thing which Canada ought to address itself to is to safeguard these great water powers for Canadian use. Furthermore, I asserted a moment ago, and I reaffirm it now, that as a result of a discussion in this House a few years ago we prevented the export of power and (that, in my estimation, is a very vital thing to this country. I say this House ought to put beyond all peradventure the danger of a government entering into an agreement with large interests south of the line for the export of our power for the purpose of developing industry there. There should go out from Canada this declaration of Canadian policy: Bring your factories to Canadian power if you want to utilize that power for the use of those factories.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I have spoken long enough, altogether too long, much longer than I had contemplated. When the chief whip asked me how long I was going to speak I said I would speak about an hour if I were not interrupted, but that if I were interrupted I would probably take longer. These interruptions, which I welcome, usually result in the lengthening of one's speech. I will conclude wiit-h this statement:	I have endeavoured to bring into survey before this House the actions of this government, deliberate actions which they affirm. I have endeavoured to show the effect of these actions upon the trade of Canada, and I have sought to impress upon the House that it was desirable and necessary that parliament should take cognizance of these things to, as far as possible, direct the policy of this country for the development of Canada, for the expansion of our industries within Canada, and the use of our resources for the benefit of Canadians, and not develop a foreign trade or foreign industries for the benefit of other countries.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened with a great deal of attention this afternoon to the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens) while he dealt with tlhe budget as presented by the Minister of Finance a few days ago, and I noticed) that he was labouring under special difficulties. The hon. member stated that the present budget was a static or Stationary budget. A static or stationary budget can come only from a static or stationary party such as the one we have across the floor of the House. A budget brought down by the Liberal party is something different from a stationary or static proposition. It is a live-wire project. There is no doubt that at the present time in Canada the Liberal party, fundamentally speaking, stands for the same policy as the Liberal party has stood for in history. It stands for a policy of peace, retrenchment and reform; peace between one province and another in Canada fiscally, financially and every other way; retrenchment when it is possible to cut down the public expenditure and pay off the national debt, and reform- not stagnation. The party that stands for these three great principles of peace, retrenchment and reform in order to make a great Dominion, is the party that stands for a policy of action and not a policy of inaction such as that which has been handed down to us since confederation by the Tory party.
The hon. member tried to prove that our policy was one of inaction, of non-development. In 1868 the Tories were in power in Canada and our imports amounted to $37,000,000 and our exports to $17,000,000. How

The Budget-Mr. McIntosh
is that for inactivity, for a stationary condition of trade? In 1878 our imports were $37,000,000, practically "stationary," the same as in 1868, and our exports amounted to only $45,000,000, or an increase of only $8,000,000 over our imports for the same year to the motherland, as regards which our Tory friends are always fond of saying how loyal they are, how they stand for a greater empire, for greater imperial' relationships and trade. That was the condition under their rule in 1868 and 1878. These are facts and I defy anyone to contradict them.
In 1883 our imports from Great Britain amounted to $51,000,000 and our exports to $47,000,000. How is that for tying up Canada with the mother country from a commercial point of view? Not very much connection there. In 1896 our imports amounted to $32,000,000 and our exports to $47,000,000. After that we get the value of the imperial preference. In 1911 our imports amounted to $109,000,000 and our exports to $136,000,000. They go over the $100,000,000 mark for the first time in the history of Canada. In 1922 our imports amounted to $117,000,000 and our exports to $300,000,000. In 1925 our imports amounted to $151,000,GOO and our exports to $397,000,000, or nearly the $400,000,000 mark. That is action; that is not a stationary condition of trade; that is not inactivity. There is nothing static about that. That happened during Liberal rule under the leadership of Sir Wilfrid Laurier. The British preference was introduced by the Liberal party in 1897. The Tories talked about it for twenty-five years, and yet after all their talk about loyalty, patriotism and imperialism, they were afraid to concede the preference on certain goods in order to link up Canada with the empire.
The bon. member made another statement as regards which the facts are absolutely against him. He said that the Liberal party was divided on the Duncan report. I characterize that as an absolute falsehood. That is not true. No hon. member should rise in this House and make such statements. A member ought to size up his office honourably from the point of view of his riding, his province and the Dominion. When a man gets up and makes a statement of that kind that he knows to be untrue, that he cannot back up with the facts, he is doing something altogether out of place. The fact is that the Liberal party, when that question comes up in the House, will stand undivided; it will stand united. The hon. member in discussing this question before it comes up in the House, is endeavouring to make political capital out of a matter that deeply concerns the Dominion. I would deprecate

that on the part of any hon. member, I care not whether he be on this side or the other, or from one group or another group.
He further stated that there was in the Duncan report a reference to dealing with the tariff. This is the way in which the Duncan report handled the tariff question. The hon. gentleman's statement was altogether out of place. On page 32 of the report there is an item dealing with a trade treaty that was asked for as regards forest products. The Duncan report is not asking anything as regards raising or lowering the tariff on forest products. It asks for a trade treaty to be arranged on those products between the maritime provinces and the states to the south. Our maritime friends know that is true. Further we must remember that that trade treaty will be a sort of reciprocity. My hon. friend opposite belongs to the party that in 1911 went out and defeated reciprocity, lost this country millions of dollars and tore it practically asunder from coaat to coast. Yet he has the temerity, the audacity, to get up in parliament this afternoon and tell us that the Duncan report wants the matter dealt with in a tariff way when that report makes no reference to the tariff on those products. It speaks entirely about a commercial treaty which we can negotiate internationally and as regards which we shall get down to rock bottom facts and endeavour to heal the maritime situation as far as possible.
On page 33 as regards the fish trade, the maritime report is asking for a trade treaty between the maritimes and the republic to the south of us. That is practically the same proposition. If we go further we shall see just how foolish the hon. member's statements are. On page 36 we find something about coal, a customs tariff on coal, of which we have heard a great deal in this House. The Duncan report states that the coal question ought to be brought before the tariff board. When it is brought before the tariff board we shall get all the facts; .they will investigate the proposition fully and lay the facts before parliament, and we as representatives of the Canadian people will decide on a policy in regard to the question of coal. What is wrong about that? I do not think there is anything wrong. On page 37 we get what the Duncan report says in regard to steel. The statement there is to the effect that the whole question of steel-and. that is an important question in Canada and particularly important in the maritimes-in all its fulness should be placed before this commission. We should get the facts in regard to it as well as the facts in regard to coal

The Budget-Mr. McIntosh
and act accordingly. So that as fa<r as the statement of the hon. member with reference to the Duncan report is concerned, that it deals entirely with the raising or the lowering of the tariff on certain materials, the truth is that the report makes no statement. There is to be no raising or lowering of the tariff on coal or steel until there has been investigation. On the other two items, forest products and fish, nothing is said about the tariff; it aims at simply dealing internationally with these difficulties.
My hon. friend admits that throughout Canada the Robb budget has attracted a great deal of attention east and west. The publications in this country, province by province and district by district, have told the people that this is a splendid budget. What are the facts? Will hon. gentlemen tell me that the average publisher of a daily or a weekly newspaper, after reading the budget, sizing it up and analysing the effect of it, will publish in his paper anything that he does not think is true? He wants to place before his readers the facts. If the budget is an encouraging one he will say so, and if it is not encouraging he will ktate to the contrary. I believe our newspaper publishers, irrespective of politics or irrespective of whether they are weeklies or dailies, take a presentation of this kind and analyse it carefully; after it is analysed they reach certain conclusions, and that is what they have done in this instance. That being the case we have positive proof that the budget is a proper one. It has received a splendid reception from east to west, and the Robb budget of this year is known throughout Canada, as was the one of last year, as a good budget, a budget that will be not only a cementing factor between east and west but a solidifying factor so far as the various provinces of the Dominion are concerned.
My hon. friend says that although there has been tax reduction we are taking more taxes from the people. The fact is that we have reduced taxation, and if we have taken more in taxation from the people it is not because the rates of taxation are higher; in fact they are lower, but we have done more business. It is a question in simple mathematics, and our friends cannot see through it. Last year the provisions of the Robb budget were presented to nine million people; the people went to the polls not long afterward, and we see the result in this House to-day. It is positive proof that so far as the people are concerned they know a good thing when they see it, and they know the 1927 budget is a good thing.
My hon. friend also, dealing with the national debt, states that we have not paid the amount we say we have paid; and he goes into a complicated discussion on the question of public accounting. The public accounts show us that last year we paid $27,000,000 off the national debt. I do not doubt that. We -are going to pay off thirty or forty millions this year. Now what have we paid off since confederation? I have the figures here. Our Conservative friends are always anxious to make out that they are wonderful financiers, that they have done the right thing by Canada, and that if returned to office they will do it again. Since confederation the national debt of Canada has been a big question for finance ministers and parties to handle; it has been an even bigger question since the war and is going to be a big question in the future. What were the reductions of the national debt made by the party to which my hon. friend belongs, about which he waxed so eloquent this afternoon when referring to the national debt? In 1871 the Tories were in power and what did they do? They cut the national debt about half a million dollars. In 1882 they cut the national debt one million and three quarters-and at the same time they added ten million dollars to it. In 1912 they were in power and they cut the national debt $125,000. The public accounts show that, and I am taking the public accounts for one party as well as for the other. What is sauce for the goose is sauce for the gander. In 1913 what did they do? They paid $25,000,000 off the national debt. In other words, they have been in power for over thirty years since confederation and all they have paid off the national debt on the whole is $27,000,000. What about the Liberal administrations? In 1900 the Liberals paid off half a million; in 1904 they paid off another half million; in 1903 they paid off $10,000,000; in 1907, $3,250,000; in 1924, $36,000,000; in 1925, $343,000; in 1926, $27,000,000, and in 1927, this year, we expect a payment of $31,000,000. In other words, since confederation the Conservatives, who have been in power longer than we were, paid $27,000,000 off the national debt as compared with a payment by the Liberals of over $100,000,000. There is the record, and I will leave it to anyone to say whether the record of the Conservative party can be characterized as an active one, or whether it should be regarded as "stationary". I would say it was a "stationary" policy and not designed for the benefit of Canada.
The hon. member for West Calgary (Mr. Bennett) suggested that we ought to conscript

The Budget-Mr. McIntosh
the money of the insurance companies and the banks to pay off the national debt. Following that up he made this statement:
I am of course only elaborating a plan that has grown in my mind after some consideration.
We a.re glad he gave it some consideration.
And it does not follow that the plan is at all sound in detail.
Did hon. members ever hear such a confession before a national House of Commons -a man rising and claiming that he has a splendid scheme for paying off the national debt of Canada, and after he has told us his objective he says it does not follow that the plan is sound in detail! We all know that a plan or a policy that is not sound in detail is absolutely worthless; consequently he might as well have saved his breath, and if that is all he has to offer we had better go on as we are. The cutting down of the national debt is a splendid work for any party or any finance minister, and I believe our hon. Minister oif Finance is entitled to the respect and admiration of the House of Commons as well as of all Canada for the introduction of his budget and the determination he haa shown in trying to lower this debt from year to year since 1923.
Further, as a Liberal I have absolute confidence in the Prime Minister and in the Minister of Finance that during the next fifteen years-and we are going to be in power that long by the way things are going now-during the next fifteen years if we continue to reduce the national debt at the present rate-and I have faith that our Minister of Finance will enable us to do this-we shall have paid off about six or seven hundred million dollars. Then should our Tory friends get into office-

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE OF THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: No.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE OF THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I do not believe they
will, of course; but suppose fate should so decree, we ought to pass legislation to compel them to pay off annually $40,000,000. That is the only way we shall ever be able to get them to reduce the national debt, otherwise they will never pay off a dollar if they can help it. Dur'ng all their terms of office since 1867 they have paid off only a paltry $27,000,000, they have run the country into debt by billions of dollars, and then they boast that they are great financiers, great Canadians, great imperialists, and that they stand for the old flag, the old emlpire and a greater Canada.
This budget is a surplus budget. The hon. Minister of Finance shows a surplus of $31,000,000, last year he had a surplus of $33,000,000. That is conclusive proof that he and his colleagues are looking after national affairs pretty
fMr. McIntosh.]
well. These recurring surpluses clearly indicate that trade is flourishing and that prudence is being exercised in the conduct of the country's affairs. If a man doses his books at the end of the year with a balance on the wrong side he is drifting towards bankruptcy, and the very fact that When the Minister of Finance closes our books at the end of the year he can show a surplus of $31,000,000 is ample evidence that Canadian trade is developing, that a buoyant spirit is abroad com-merieally and financially, that crops have been bountiful, that our transportation systems have been busy, that credit is good, that money is cheaper and easier to get, and that Canadians are awakening to the possibilities of imperial and foreign trade.
But, Mr. Speaker, we have not only a surplus budget, we have a favourable balance of trade. One of the great financial apostles of the Tory party in days gone by-it might be well if they had his peer to-day-was Sir Leonard Tilley, Sir John A. Macdonald's Minister of Finance. He was always telling his party:	If you cannot show a favourable
balance of trade you are no good; you will never get anywhere, you will never impress the people that you can govern the country, and you will not be returned to power for decades. His words are just as true to-day as when he uttered them-and the Tory party believes them, but it will not admit its belief. We have been going on from year to year showing a favourable balance of trade: this year $250,000,000; last year $401,000,COO; the year before $284,000,000-an average for the last three years of over $300,000,000 annually. That is another reason why I am glad as a citizen of Canada to stand up in this House to-day and declare that I shall vote against the amendment and for the resolution. I believe this is a popular budget, I believe it is an accurate statement of facts, I believe that the country is satisfied with it, and considering what we have gone through politically during the last two years I believe that the people as a Whole will say that the Minister of Finance has presented another outstanding budget that will demonstrate to the world that Canada is on the upgrade, and that in the years to come we are going to make history.
Some hon. members on the opposite side of the House find fault with this budget and ask:	Why not reduce the tariff? According
to their view the tariff board is an excuse for the government to delay action on the tariff.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE OF THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE OF THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
That is not true. Last
year in this House I declared that we should give the tariff board a square deal before we

The Budget-Mr. McIntosh
passed judgment on it. I say the same to-day. Every industry in all Canada that feels it has a grievance must bring that grievance before the board to be thoroughly analysed. Then let the members of this House from all Canada consider the facts on which the tariff board bases its report and act according to their best judgment. Let us do by every industry what in our opinion is honest and right. In that way alone shall we bring about a united Canada enjoying a constantly expanding trade from coast to coast. If we are going to continue our tariff, let it be a tariff fair to all. Do not let the impression go abroad that any industry can at any time go to the Minister of Finance and get the tariff raised or lowered without this House deciding exactly what that raising or lowering shall be. I still have confidence in the tariff board. I say, give it a chance to demonstrate its usefulness. Left the tariff board get busy and deal with every application that comes before it on its merits. Then we in turn will decide what ought to be done for the good of Canada as a whole.
I repeat, Mr. Speaker, that in my estimation this is one of the best budgets ever presented to the country. It will show the world that we have another surplus, that we have reduced our national debt, that public revenues are buoyant, that trade is active, and that our people from coast to coast are piling uip big trade returns year by year. That is important from the standpoint of western and eastern Canada. It will be an important factor, a magnet, in bringing the right class of immigrants to this country, and I believe we want population. It is the general feeling throughout the country that we must have more people; we need more men on the land to increase agricultural production. It is the opinion on all sides that what .is required is an intelligent colonization and agricultural development policy. We have a great opportunity now to develop the wonderful heritage which is ours, and we should do so rationally, with the interests of the people in view as well as for the benefit of those who are to come.
What about our population? In 1871 we had a population of 3,370,000; in 1900 this had increased to a little over 5,000,000 and in 1921 it was 8,800.000. In other words, we have brought into the country since 1870, 4,500,000 people. Taking the population of 1870 and working out the natural increase at two and a quarter per cent per annum we find, with a total increase of 4.500,000 freer abroad that our population in 1921 instead of being about 9,000.000 ought to have been
over 16,000,000. For that 4,500,000 people whom we brought into Canada, the government spent $24,000,000 or $6 per head. That seems to me to be rather cheap. Economists tell us that the capital productive value to the state of the average individual is $3,000, and we have brought in over 4,500,000 at $6 a head and have not been able to hold them. The natural increase has not been what it should have been. We have lost many of our people and our problem is twofold: we must first get the people, and in the second place we have to retain them. That is a vital question.
It seems to me that we have a lop-sided-development in Canada so far as our population is concerned. The people are rushing off the land into the urban centres and to a large extent they are going to the United States. In 1925, in one month, over 8.000 Canadians crossed the border. That works out at the rate of 100,000 a year. During the last nine months 48,000 Canadians have come back, and with good times and increased prosperity in trade, together with a forward-looking policy on the part of this government, thousands more will return. These people will probably go on the land, and we should do our best to hold them with a view to increasing our agricultural production. In Russia 85 per cent of the people are on the land and 15 per cent in the urban centres; in the United States 72 per cent dwell in the cities and 28 per cent on the land; in Canada in the year 1870 we had 69 per cent of the population on the land. In 1901 our rural population was 63 per cent, but in 1921 it had gone down to 50 per cent. This proves beyond question that we need more people; there is no overproduction on the land. It proves further, as I say, that we have a lop-sided policy which we must rectify, and the problem for Canadians to grapple with to-day is to obtain the right class of people to go on the land, to balance agricultural production with our industrial activities and so bring about that happiness in the rural communities which will make for a unified industrial and agricultural life in Canada. The very basis of this problem lies in arriving at the proper equilibrium or normal balance between the country and the urban population, and with that end in view we should devise a policy whereby we may be able to develop our agricultural areas to their utmost, at the same time maintaining urban development. We have 358,000.000 acres of arable land in Canada. In 1870, 36.000.000 acres were occupied, in 1901. 63.000,000 acres and in 1921, 145,000,000. But what about cultivation? In 1870 we had 10,000,000 acres under cultivation: in 1901, 20,000,000 acres, and in

speechtext:
But my objection
still stands; the effect is to assist the railways to bring in these immigrants, and my point is that if the immigrant is worth so much to the railways why should we go out of our way to assist the railways to lower their rates to bring immigrants here?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE OF THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I think the railways are assisting us; it is a straight business proposition and they are cooperating with us and with the British government in order to get more men on the land. In Canada wo have the land and in Great Britain they have the men, and the proposition is to bring the two together for the good of both countries.
I diid not intend to speak so long, Mr. Speaker, but in closing I would like to repeat that I think this budget is important to every riding in Canada, and for the life of me I cannot see why there should be much opposition to it in the House. I know that the budget is already popular in my riding; I am satisfied it is popular all over Saskatchewan; I know it is popular in Manitoba and I am sure that the rank and file of the people of Alberta will accept it if they are given the facts in a clear and straightforward manner. I believe this budget is popular across the mountains as well as in Ontario and throughout the east, and for that reason I feel that it will have
a unifying effect in bringing about a greater nation. I am going to support it not only as a representative of my own riding but because I am a western member and because of the fact that not only am I supposed to do my best for my own riding in this House but I am Supposed to consider the interests of Canada, and I think this budget will link the sections of this country into a more splendid and united whole. I believe it will be a factor in bringing to Canada the people we want and in making our agricultural and colonization policy more successful than ever. For these reasons and many others, Mr. Speaker, I intend to support the resolution of the Minister of Finance.
