maintopic: MONTREAL, OTTAWA AND GEORGIAN BAT CANAL COMPANY

speechtext: Mr. E. R. E. CHEVRIER (Ottawa) moved the second reading of Bill No. 78 respecting the Montreal, Ottawa and Georgian Bay Company.

maintopic: MONTREAL, OTTAWA AND GEORGIAN BAT CANAL COMPANY
speechtext: I would ask the promoter of this bill to let it stand. It is only a few minutes now before the time for discussion of private bills expires and there are some members on this side who would like to discuss the bill.

maintopic: MONTREAL, OTTAWA AND GEORGIAN BAT CANAL COMPANY
speechtext:
I should like to oblige
the hon. member although of course, Mr. Speaker, I am entirely in your hands. I admit that there are quite a number of members on both sides of the House who would like to take part in the discussion of the bill, but I submit that the proper place for the discussion would be in the railway committee to which the bill would be referred after its second reading here. No harm could result. The discussion would take place there as freely as in this committee, and as I have observed on both sides of the House a desire to expedite the business of the session I think considerable time would be saved if my hon. friend would allow the second reading.

maintopic: MONTREAL, OTTAWA AND GEORGIAN BAT CANAL COMPANY
speechtext:
I know it is not customary to speak at any length on private bills, but this is one occasion on which I certainly think we should discuss the principle of the measure before us. If we pass the second reading of the bill the House will be virtually assenting to the principle involved. It is true the bill will be referred to the committee on railways and canals, where its details will be discussed, and will then come back to this House for further consideration in our own committee. But, I repeat, the second reading of the bill is tantamount to an approval of its principle.
The project of a canal on the Ottawa and French rivers has been before the public for many years, the original bill for the canal having been passed in the year 1894, long before any of us were members of the House. One of the first things that came up for discussion in the House after I had the honour of becoming one of its members was this same Georgian Bay canal bill. At that time the whole of the Ottawa valley was very much interested in the project, from which we hoped many things. Many elections, if they were not run solely on the question of the Georgian Bay canal, had at any rate a substantial relation to it; the subject was a factor in all of the elections in this Ottawa valley during a number of years. We all hoped and expected that the canal would be built. What has happened, however? The charter has been renewed fourteen times. The matter has been on the statute books since 1894, some thirty-two years, and so far nothing practical has been done.
I want it distinctly understood that I am not in any way opposed to the building of this canal, if those who are behind it actually want to build the canal and are not asking for a renewal of the charter for any other purpose. I do not think we need this canal as much as it was needed years ago, because in the meantime we have enlarged the Welland canal and some day we may enlarge the St. Lawrence canal. While years ago we felt that this would be a new outlet for grain from the northwest, vessels now carrying grain on the great lakes have become so much larger and the depth of water provided by the Welland canal so much greater that as a practical matter it does not seem to me that this Georgian bay canal is quite as essential as formerly. At the same time, if any body of gentlemen are willing to put up their money for this canal I would not suggest that they be not allowed to do so, and I am quite sure no member of this House would not be happy to have this canal built for the benefit

The Budget-Mr. Evans
of the interior navigation of this country in bringing grain from the northwest and also in distributing the various products of the Ottawa valley. This is a rich valley and its resources have hardly been scratched as yet; not only is there timber and pulpwood, but minerals are being discovered continually, and it is possible that the Georgian bay canal might pay. So if any gentlemen wish to build it I have no objection whatever.
With regard to the promoters of this bill, I notice that in the copy on my file no promoters are mentioned, so I take it that the promoters are those named in the last renewal. My memory takes me back to the time when McLeod1 Stewart, who was a valued citizen of Ottawa, took up this idea with enthusiasm and tried to interest people in it. He did not have sufficient means to undertake the enterprise, and after some years Sir Robert Perks took up the matter. He was and still is a prominent English contractor who had built large works in various parts of the world and had made a success of his business, and a prominent man in the commercial life of London whom I often met when I had the honour of representing Canada there. Sir Robert Perks and his associates took hold of this charter and had it renewed, then employed a staff of engineers to make plans for the canal. I am not sure that they carried those plans all the way through, but certain sections of the Ottawa river were plotted out by a small staff engaged for that purpose. Then what happened? The money was not forthcoming, and they could not build the canall. They came to this House asking for a renewal of the charter time and time again; in fact this charter has become a hardy perennial. I think Sir Robert Perks came to Ottawa every year in those days to interview first Sir Wilfrid Laurier during his years of office and then Sir Robert Borden, and his energetic endeavours were only interrupted by the war. He wanted the Dominion government to guarantee the bonds of this canal, arguinig that this was really a public work for the public advantage, and that therefore the Dominion government should guarantee the bonds of the company. The promoters claimed that if the government did that they would never have to pay a cent because the revenues would be sufficient to pay the cost of operation and also to cover the interest on the bonds issued.
My reason for stating these facts is that even Sir Robert Perks, who was known in London as the head of a powerful group of financiers and who had built with his associates large works in various parts of the world, did not find himself in a position to provide the money necessary to build this canal without a government guarantee. If that was the case with this powerful group of financiers in England1, in the first place I would like to know where the money is to come from to build this canal now, because it is going to cost twice as much as it would have then cost. That is the first question I would like to bring forward for the consideration of the House, but it is by no means my main reason for bringing up these matters on the second reading of this bill. This is not a party question in any sense of the word, but we have three or more groups in this House and if a few businesslike words from me on the. question of this renewal would enable those members from different parts of Canada to give careful consideration to this whole question, when the matter comes up in committee I will try my best to impart that information.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I have to go into the matter of water power in connection with this bill and I would therefore call your attention to the fact that it is 9 o'clock. I would like to continue, however, when the matter comes up again.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

speechtext: The House resumed the debate on the motion of Hon. J .A. Robb (Minister of Finance) that Mr. Speaker do now leave the chair for the House to go into committee of ways and means, and the proposed amendment thereto of Mr. Coote.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the budget has each year come to be looked upon as a register of progress, or otherwise, regarding trade. It is also an indication of the policy of the government, and looking at it from this standpoint the government has evidently been careful in the present budget about one thing only. Its one concern has been for the payment of dividends on capital investments, rather than for easing the burden of the high cost of living on the worker of the nation.
In this connection I wish to say a word regarding a statement made by the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens) this afternoon. He says that the policy he stands for would maintain the very highest standard of living possible. But he would put the whole burden of the high cost of living and the decent standard of living on the
The Budget-Mr. Evans

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
We shall have to go back to flints.
The Budget-Mr. Evans

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I had hoped, as time went
on, with the splendid opportunity that this government had of restoring its party to principle, that a greater proportion of taxes would eadh year be collected by the direct method; but the primary producer is still to be the beast of burden and the whole farm is to be directed from Ottawa.
I do not think I would have spoken on the budget to-night, but for one or two reasons. I want to voice my surprise and indignation that both in the budget speech and in the reply of the hon. member for West Calgary (Mr. Bennett) there is the boasted prosperity of the city and urban industries, while the great basic industry, agriculture, is simply bankrupt. I am mortified at the contempt with which the agriculturist of the Dominion is treated year after year. It is true there is some $380,000 increase in the estimates for agriculture this year. What will that be for? To create some white collar jobs and to duplicate the work of the provinces in research and so on. It will go for the winter fair in Toronto too.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The vote is not increased.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
But as to the man on the
land, who finds the price of his product against the competition of all the world, there is nothing in this budget for him. Nothing is done to bring the cost of production in line with world's prices. I want to say to-day that manufacturing in Canada as it is carried on under a system of protection is a national canker which is eating at the vitals of true industry. It cannot either supply the home market or manufacture for export except as it leans on the politician. Politics is a screaming farce, behind which the legalized robbery is carried on. John Charlton, a member of this House a good many years ago, speaking in this chamber on March 18, 1879, said:
I venture to say. . . that these monopolies which the government is now aiding to build up will not be easily removed.
He went further and said:
It will perhaps take more than one verdict of the people of this country to unloosen that grip which will fasten on them with a death-like tenacity.
And now, after nearly fifty years have passed, the government in the presentation of this budget has thrown out a distinct challenge to the primary producers of this country and to everybody who has still left a little sense of liberty and justice.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The Minister of Railways
(Mr. Dunning) surprised me last night.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Surprised
me too.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
It is not many years since
I sat with the Minister of Railways on the board of the Grain Growers' Association of Saskatchewan. He and I together, and others helped to draft that clause in the Canadian Council of Agriculture platform calling for freer trade, demanding an increase in the British preference to bring about complete free trade with England in five years. What now? I want to say to this House that besides the economic feature of this question there is also another side to it, the moral side, and I want to quote no less an authority than George Brown, who many years ago founded the Toronto Globe. He used these words:
If a public man avows certain principles, agitates those principles and seeks to establish those principles and when he attains power laughs at his professions and casts his principles to the winds, he is aiming a blow at political morality.
The Minister of Railways made an authoritative statement last night as coming from the government. They are going to work for free trade, but they are going to do it in a cautious way. He made exactly the same statement last night that Sir Wilfrid Laurier made in 1896. They proceeded cautiously. By 1904 the Liberal government had succeeded so far that they placed soft soap and false teeth on the free list.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
And last year they put
angostura bitters on the free list.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
And the same year they
placed on the statute book of this country What is known as the anti-dumping act, the most diabolical legislation that had hitherto been thought of in any country. We were the first to enact that law. Canada has led the way in special privilege. She is still leading it, and I say this: that even in the United States alongside of us, with her high tariff, a country we are exhorted by a part of this House to emulate or to attain to the same privileged position, their people are not burdened by class privilege to-day as much as the worker and primary producer in Canada is. I hope that western Canada at least will take particular notice of the retrograde step the government has taken this year. Because of the reform which was foreshadowed in the fatal session of last year, and the promises of the Liberal government, only one protectionist was elected in the three prairie provinces, a fact that the government has treated

The Budget-Mr. Evans
entirely with contempt. Then, as if it were not enough to maintain the duties on the necessaries of life at the old rate, an order in council was passed on the 25th of November, 1926, which legalized the application of 47a of the Customs "Act, which allowed a valuation on certain natural products in keeping with the seasonal and the regional importation, at the instigation of the fruit and vegetable dealers. The Minister of Railways (Mr. Dunning) last night did not know anything about 47a. I wonder who passed this order in council. It was placed on the statute book on June 22, 1922, during the first session that the Liberal party came into power aftei the war. Even the leader of the opposition at that time was startled by it; protectionist as he was, he was shocked.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Protection gone mad.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Let me quote his words. He said:
I do not know whether this is fully understood or not by the hon. gentlemen to my left,-
meaning the Progressives.
-but I admit that it is fully understood by me. This provision is protection personified. This is the last emanation from the government that denounced protection two or three days ago. For purposes of valuation the minister can fix the value where he likes, and any basis he likes, on any principle he likes, to suit any interest he likes, as low as he likes, as high as he likes, and when he likes. In a word, this simply puts into the power of the minister the whole elevation of the tariff of this country.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Whom are you quoting?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The Right Hon. Arthur Meighen, speaking in this House on the sight of June 22, 1922. It is more than likely that 47a is applied according to the wishes of the Canadian packers and the needs of political parties. In fact I have looked on 47a during all these years as simply an advertisement for tenders. I say to you gentlemen of the House of Commons to-night that otherwise it is not conceivable that the duty would be increased by a false valuation on these natural products to as high as 156f per cent as was the case this past summer.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Adequate protection 1

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The duty on a carload of
tomatoes was raised from $150 to $385 by a false valuation. As I have said before in this House, I cannot understand even a protectionist trading on the rights of the consumers of Canada in this way without some consideration. I cannot. I have always
spoken frankly on this question, and I cannot look on this in any other way. An increase of 156-f per cent by a false valuation! Just consider what it means on an article of diet that ought to be on everybody's table all the year around if possible. And there was no indication at the time that fruit was being dumped in Canada from the United States. No one could say there was. No evidence has ever been adduced to show that there was any dumping of fruit or vegetables at that time..
When the member for Weyburn (Mr. Young) was speaking a couple of days ago he informed1 the House that he took some trouble to get evidence regarding dumping, and went from one department to another. He is still minus the evidence. I knew he could not get it, I had been on the same rounds before. I say to-night, it is strange that even a protectionist would want to increase the cost of living to the worker in this way, seeing that it must inevitably entail a demand for higher wages. Why has it been done so long? Because the whole burden has been passed on to the farmers of this country, who are now bankrupt.
One of the chief arguments for protection is the necessity of preserving a high standard of living. But in this budget the government has retained all the taxes on the necessaries of life. Surely when the drop in revenue has been used to make the rich richer, we cannot be deceived as to the policy of import penalties and the purpose of those who control industry and politics throughout the Dominion. This 47a is one of the most pernicious pieces of legislation that has ever been enacted. I assert, Sir, that it is nothing but fraud and graft and intrigue and injustice. Yes, it was first invoked when two elections were called within one year. What does it mean?
There is another feature regarding this dumping clause. I say it is particularly annoying at this time when we are sending the Hon. Vincent Massey to Washington to bring about better trade relations with the United States. Especially is that better feeling desirable by reason of the live stock condition all over Canada to-day. But the Minister of Customs has seen fit to pin-prick Uncle Sam in this way, and thus he has forestalled for many years to come any good that we may expect from the Hon. Vincent Massey's ambassadorship.
I have said th-at manufacturing, as it is carried on in this country to-day, is a canker on our national progress, and I am wondering how long that part of the population engaged

The Budget-Mr. Evans

in primary production will see fit to pay tribute to a privileged class to concentrate the earnings of the workers and create an aristocracy in our cities. Manufacture is a canker for the reason that the manufacturing class admit that a protective tariff is needed to keep out foreign competition. This tariff is maintained chiefly for two reasons: The manufacturer must have the privilege of naming the price to the home consumer; and that price must be high enough to ensure a profit on the whole of his output, both domestic and export. And the tariff is being used for that purpose. Is it any wonder, then, that the farmers of this country at last are in rebellion against such a system? I have said before in this House, and it will not do any harm to repeat it, that the farmer is exploited on the finished products from the very farm itself. For example, the very grade of Hour that we are buying to-day in Saskatoon, where the wheat is hauled into the hoppers of the big mills, and no tariff or freight rates are involved, is dearer by 20 to 30 cents for a 98-pound sack than it is on the other side of the Atlantic. That is what protection is doing for us.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: On the same flour?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: On the same flour, yes. They tell us that it is not the same quality. I know that they do not ship poor flour to Britain; Britain gets the best flour that can be procured in the world. They cannot sell poor stuff there.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Nor in Saskatoon either.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Perhaps not. Our manufacturers to-day will sell against all competitors in foreign markets the very goods for which they charge us so much higher prices, and the fallacy of protection was never better illustrated than it is in the fact that goods made in Canada are sold cheaper in the markets of the world than they are at home. When the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Malcolm) was speaking the other day, he undertook to contradict what he considered a wrong impression. He referred to a list of goods quoted, I think, by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) at page 393 of Hansard'. These things coming into Canada "for further manufacture" and on which no duty is paid represented a total value last year of $224,000,060. I want to point out in this connection what constitutes a real injustice. All raw material for manufacture, of the same nature produced on the farms of Canada, comes into this country free of duty. Not only have we to meet the competition of the

world's markets in the sale of hides, but on the finished article, harness, boots, shoes and so forth, and all manufactures of leather, the farmer must pay an enhanced price because of the import penalty on these goods amounting in some cases to over one-third of their value. Wool, for example, is on the free list for manufacturers' use; but the primary producer, who has no protection for himself on anything he produces, pays at least 35 per cent of a duty in the way of enhanced price because of the import penalty on all woollen clothing. The same is true of other articles. Rubber, for instance, is free for the manufacturer. I have a list oif such goods here, but I will not take the trouble of reading it to the House. All these things come in free for the manufacturers' use, and we do not get any advantage in the way of reduced prices. We are charged, I repeat, an enhanced price as a result of the penalty imposed on the imports.
It is impossible for things to go on much longer in this way. Under this system of class privilege in the United States agriculture has been reduced to a state of bankruptcy, and both here and across the border the one great problem for the agriculturist to-day is how to free himself from the compact that exists -between the politicians and the manufacturers and distributors. This compact is responsible for the present impoverished condition of the maritime provinces, which must shortly be dealt with. Unless, therefore, the trade policy of the Dominion is rectified, no relief given in a direct way to those provinces will make them any better off than they are now. A feature of this system which is worthy of notice at this time, seeing that the maritimes are before us for redress, is that the concentration of wealth and industry is regional. Our problems and our grievances are regional. The density of population is a problem to-day in our cities, and the concentration of wealth and industry has eliminated the m-an whose capital is a little money and plenty of brawn and muscle. This type of man is reduced to the position of a wage earner. That is why I say that enterprise is being destroyed under the present system.
The hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Manion), speaking the other day, cited the fact that we have already invested in life insurance $4,500,000,000; and he mentioned this to show how prosperous we are. I say that this -is no sign of prosperity. It is simply the result of the concentration of wealth and industry. When the -man in a small way is forced out of his little business and becomes a wage earner, all he cares to do is to keep up a life policy, thereby further forging the

The Budget-Mr. Odette
fetters in which he is labouring at present- the concentration of wealth and industry. Even life insurance to-day has become an evil in this way, and I want to warn the workers, who are using their earnings to concentrate wealth thus, that there will come a point rvhere even this will be unsafe. Why? Because the base on which privilege to-day rests is giving way. The primary producer, who has to bring in most of the income of the nation, by marketing his products in competition with the rest of the world is facing ruin. Our capitalists to-day are seeking investments in foreign countries. Their surplus profits are going abroad instead of being kept at home to develop our own natural resources and to provide work for our own workmen.
One great sign of the times is seen in the fact that one of our leading economists, Professor Goforth of McGill University, the other day advocated the importation of some thousands of Chinese under a system of indentured labour for the purpose of developing our natural resources because the wages of our workingmen cannot be made commensurate with the cost of living, which has been steadily driven up. Whose fault is it? It is the fault of the system; and the professor's remedy, I know, is uneconomic and inhuman. But it is significant as showing that even the capitalists of the Dominion to-day are up against it. They are up against the problem which the agriculturist has felt for several years back.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Everybody is broke.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The hon. gentleman says everybody is broke. His remark is intended to be sarcastic. Surely there is no need for us to have any great economist tell us the simple rules of economy. I tell the hon. gentleman we are digging our own grave. They say that protection is high in the United States and is a tremendous price fixing power for the manufacturer there. If that is so, why has smuggling from that high protectionist country become so popular? It is a most profitable business to-day to go to the United States and load up with silks and woollens for Canada.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Tell us how it is
done.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Perhaps if the hon. gentleman got on his feet sometimes he would know more about it than I do. I know what he is hinting at, that the smuggling is made possible by the nefarious trade in liquor from this Dominion into that friendly country, and 32649-43J
I say again that therein we are defying the laws of the United States and also violating the spirit of the treaty entered into last year in regard to this matter. Senator Smith, of South Carolina, speaking in the United States Senate the other day, showed that agriculturists in the United States are in exactly the same condition as those in Canada. He said there had been much talk about prosperity, which members of the "old guard" were sure was unparalleled and due entirely to the Coolidge economy. When Senator Smith claimed the floor he spoke with much feeling, and after calling attention to the tremendous prosperity of Wall street and the huge volume of collateral loans of the federal reserve banks, he said that the prosperity of Wall street meant foreclosures on the farms of the United States. I have here a clipping from the Saskatoon Star of December 10, 1926, in which it is said:
Herbert Hoover, Secretary of Commerce in President Coolidge's cabinet, issued a report recently in which lie declares that the United States is enjoying a standard of living "far above that in most other countries of the world at this or any other time."
The clipping refers to a remark by Senator Brookhart, and goes on to say:
According to the Senator, who is one of the insurgent party at Washington, one million farmers in the United States have lost their homes during the Harding and Coolidge administrations, which is to say, since 1920. An independent New York weekly, The Nation, commenting on his statement says the United States is "now seeing the fine flowering of the protective tariff system which has exalted manufacturing at the expense of agriculture." This is the system which has been advocated for Canada. The object lesson of the United States should not be lost on Canadians.
We are in exactly the same condition today, and these conditions are Dominionwide. We have a beautiful country here, but equality of status as between classes and between provinces must be brought about. It does not take anyone with a gift of prophecy to say that it will not be long until confederation itself will go to pieces under this great syetem of class privilege.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise with considerable trepidation to make my first speech, if it may be so termed, on the floor of this House, and I crave the indulgence of Your Honour and of hon. members if I violate the rules of the House in any way. I can assure you that if I do transgress, my transgressions will not be wilful but due to my lack of knowledge of the time-honoured customs of this body.
The Budget-Mr. Odette

At the outset of my remarks, which I will endeavour to make brief, I desire to compliment the Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) on the budget introduced into this House last week. To be able to reduce taxation and at the same time announce a reduction in the net debt of this country is, I submit, no mean accomplishment. This afternoon the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens) argued that the reduction in the net debt meant nothing and that the only thing which counted was the funded indebtedness or, as he put it, the mortgage debt. Looking at it from a business point of view may I submit that if a manufacturing industry finds it necessary to build an addition to take care of increased business and finds it necessary to issue bonds or place a mortgage on the new addition, and if at the end of the year the financial statement shows that the profits have been increased by virtue of this addition, although the mortgage placed on the assets may have made the funded indebtedness higher, the common stockholders will benefit because these increased profits are divided among the common stockholders of that company. So, Sir, I submit that when the net debt of this country is lowered and a reduction in taxation follows, the stockholders of this country, who are the people of the country, are given dividends in the shape of reduced taxation.
While on the matter of business, some of the hon. gentlemen across the floor expressed great fear of American domination through American investments in this country. I have no such fear. I hold in my hand a copy of the Detroit Free Press dated September 22, 1926, in which appears an advertisement which I did not see in any of the newspapers in Canada. This advertisement reads as follows:
You insure your life, your house, furniture, automobile. Here is an opportunity to buy an insured investment.
This company is called the Manufacturers' Finance Corporation Limited, incorporated under the laws of the Dominion of Canada. May I ask the hon. member for Vancouver Centre, with his well known business ability and his knowledge of finance, what constitutes an insured investment? The hon. member is silent; he is a director of this company and his name appears in the directorate as Hon. H. H. Stevens, Minister of Trade and Commerce, Canadian government. Apparently that is thought insufficient and his name appears again as Hon. H. H. Stevens, ex-Minister of Trade and Commerce-and still he cannot answer what is an insured investment.
rMr. Odette.]

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: As you, Mr. Speaker, know very well, I have no right to make replies to questions across the floor of the House, but I can -certainly tell my bon. friend all about insured investments if it would be of any interest to give that information.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I believe the time is
opportune when this House should introduce and pass some legislation that would prohibit hon. members of this House from using thedr positions as members of parliament to go to the United States or to other foreign countries and solicit funds there for wildcat oil schemes in Canada.
Dealing with the reductions in taxation announced by the Minister of Finance, I believe that the abolition of the graded tax on cheques, bills of exchange and notes has been received with favour by all business men of Canada. My hon. friends in the southeast corner of the House argue that this *reduction in taxation does not benefit the mass of people. Well, let me say this to them-that when the burden of taxation is removed from the shoulders of a business man, and when the cost of doing business is lessened, that man is enabled to sell his products to the consumer for a lower price, and when the price is lowered naturally the people in general benefit.
Coming to the reduction in the taxation on matches, I disagree with the hon. member who has just taken his seat (Mr. Evans) when he says that the people of Canada do not complain about the price of matches. I know that in my part of the country they do complain of the price of matches. In Detroit, Michigan, six boxes of matches, that is of the large size containing five hundred matches each, can be purchased for the sum of twenty-five cents, while across the river in the city of Windsor, two boxes of matches cost twenty-five cents. Now the lumber from which these matches are made comes to a very large degree from the forests of Canada, and the containers that hold these matches are made from Canadian pulp. Then why should we in Canada pay three times as much for our matches as do the people of the United States? I submit that if the manufacturers of the matches are hiding behind this tax, the tax should be removed in its entirety.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Will the hon. gentleman
permit a remark?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Yes.

The Budget-Mr. Odette
Mr. EVAiN&:	I did not say the cost of
matches was sufficiently low. What I objected to was that the tax was lowered in such a way that the reduction would not be passed on to the consumer.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Well, I think time will
show whether that is true or not. I sincerely hope that time will show that this reduction has been passed on to the .purchasers of matches.
Certainly no one can find fault with the removal of the tax on bank overdrafts o,r advances by banks. It has always seemed to me somewhat of an injustice to tax the man or the industry that was forced to borrow money.
Mr. RY'CKMAN:	Your own party put it
on.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Then I presume our party will take it off, because I believe they will be here for some time to come.
Referring to the reduction in the sales tax, I desire to compliment the Minister of Finance. I believe it is a step in the right direction, but I should like to suggest to the minister that the sales tax on all Canadian-made goods be removed in its entirety, but that the sales tax on imported articles be retained.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Oh, oh.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Come over and join
us.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Hon. gentlemen opposite
applaud that suggestion. They may hurl at me the epithet that was hurled at the hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce-that I am a protectionist. Well, if that enunciation proclaims me a protectionist I am willing to be called a protectionist or any other name that my hon. friends may devise. If, by the removal of this sales tax on Canadian made goods, the citizens of Canada would be enabled to buy goods at a lower price, provided they were Canadian made and would, at the same time be able to buy the imported article without having the price increased one cent, then I say it is a good policy.
Let me go further. I sat in the gallery when the Minister of Finance told hon. gentlemen opposite that he proposed removing the excise tax of five per cent on motor cars costing $1,200 or less, and that if the manufacturers did not pass that saving on to the buyers of motor cars he would immediately remove the five per cent excise tax on cars imported from the United States or other countries. By removing the sales tax on
all Canadian made goods, but leaving it on the imported articles the Minister of Finance would have a dub with which he could force the Canadian manufacturer to pass that saving on to the consumers in Canada.
The hon. member for West Calgary (Mr. Bennett), speaking the other afternoon, said this:
My hon. friends opposite are more concerned with foreign trade, and we are more concerned with domestic trade.
As to that I would say this: In the year 1921, when the Meighen government was in power, the imports of manufactured goods into Canada exceeded our exports by $264,000,000, and in 1926 the exports of Canadian manufactured goods exceeded our imports by $23,864,000. So that in 1921 we did a foreign business but it was on the wrong side of the ledger. To-day that foreign business has been increased but the balance is on the right side of the ledger. Even if the Canadian manufacturers had the entire Canadian field to themselves they would still be behind according to these figures. Let me give you an instance of how this would work. The Ford Motor Company of Canada sell every Ford car they possibly can in Canada. Their arrangement with the American Ford company gives them the entire Canadian field, and so the potential demand here for Ford cars is filled by the Canadian Ford company. At the present moment the Ford Motor Company of Canada are employing 6,130 men, and 40 per cent of their production is exported. I ask hon. gentlemen opposite where 2,452 men would find employment if it were not for the export trade of that one company?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: What is the argument?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The argument is this, that by making reciprocal trade agreements with other countries that are beneficial to Canada, but in a spirit of give and take, industry will be built up in Canada, and I submit that one of the most beneficial things to Canada at the present moment would be a reciprocal trade agreement with the United States. If hon. members across the floor of the House would only devise ways and means of convincing the Canadian people that they should buy nothing but Canadian-made goods, and should buy no imported goods whatsoever, I am sure the manufacturers of Canada would be very thankful to them indeed. Why, in the galleries of this House we find angle iron stamped "Carnegie, Pittsburg." I do not think this government was responsible for
The Budget-Mr. Odette

the construction of this building. I believe that any Canadian government, no matter whether it be Liberal, Conservative or Progressive, should set an example and buy nothing but Canadian-made goods wherever possible, buying imported goods only when Canadian made goods are not procurable.
The hon. member for West Calgary spoke of unemployment in Vancouver.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Just before the hon.
member proceeds, I would point out that the pens on the members' desks were purchased in the United States. I believe the Liberal government is responsible for that.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
If there are pens manufactured in Canada, I think this government or any other government should buy Canadian-made pens.
I was about to remark that I am not very conversant with industrial conditions in Vancouver, but I am conversant with employment and industrial conditions in my own constituency, and I desire to say that on December 31, 1926, there were 574 more men employed in the border cities than there were on the corresponding date in 1925-and that in the face of the employment situation in the city of Detroit, dynamic Detroit, a city famous the world over for its industrial activity. Let me give you the employment figures in the city of Detroit on the same dates. On December 31, 1926, there were 41,262 fewer men employed by the manufacturers and other employers in the city of Detroit than on the corresponding date in 1925. I have heard hon. gentlemen quote in this debate Adam Smith and Stephen Leacock, and I venture to say that if this debate continues long enough, some hon. gentlemen will be quoting King Tut. Allow me to quote an industrial leader in Canada, W. R. Campbell, vice-president and general manager of the Ford Motor Company of Canada. Speaking at a dinner given by the border chambers of commerce at Windsor on January 6, 1927, he said:
I am most optimistic over the outlook for 1927. Having recently returned from an extensive tour of the Dominion, I find that financial, economic and industrial conditions throughout the country to-day are very encouraging. In every province there are indications of expanding business and prosperity. After completing this tour I am amazed at the potential buying power of Canada to-day. I have been through Canada on previous occasions, but was none too enthusiastic. This time, however, I saw- improved buying and absorption power.
The industrial situation in Canada shows a decided improvement. It is on the headv'ay made last year, and from our internal research, that we are contemplating a 20 per cent increase in our production during 1927.

I have given you the employment figures of the border cities. They speak for themselves.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Is this not in your opinion
simply a matter of advertising? This firm is in competition with other concerns selling automobiles in this country.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
All right. The Willys-
Overland Company of Toronto have increased their production by 30 per cent.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Is that not advertising too?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I do not know that this
is advertising particularly.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Why, certainly, it is advertising.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
All right. There are 574
more men employed in the border cities today than there were a year ago, so if advertising brings business to my constituency, I say let the advertising continue.
In conclusion, may I say to the hon. Minister of Finance that if he is able to bring down similar budgets providing for a reduction in taxation during the succeeding years of this parliament, he will have an augmented following behind him when the people of Canada are called upon for a pronouncement.
